tracks.tagline: Build a small C++ command-line tool that stores and searches records, learning core language features and the STL along the way.

1.title: Structs, Functions and a Console Menu
1.goal: Write a C++ program that stores a list of student records in memory and lets you add and print them from a text menu. This gets your toolchain working and practises the basics every later week builds on.
learn: Compiling and running a C++ program from the terminal (`g++`)
`struct` to group related data together
`std::vector` to store a growing list of records
Passing data by reference (`&`) to avoid copies
A simple menu loop with `switch` and `std::cin`
steps: Install a C++ compiler (g++ via MinGW/WSL, or use an online compiler first) and confirm `g++ --version` works.
Define a `struct Student { std::string name; int roll; double marks; };`.
Create a `std::vector<Student>` to hold all records and write an `addStudent` function that pushes a new one onto it.
Write a `printAll(const std::vector<Student>&)` function that prints a neat table.
Build a menu loop: `1) Add  2) Show All  3) Quit`, reading choices with `std::cin`.
Validate input: if `roll` or `marks` entry fails (e.g. text where a number is expected), clear the error and ask again instead of crashing.
Compile with `g++ -Wall -Wextra -o toolkit main.cpp` and fix every warning it shows.
Commit your code with a short README explaining how to build and run it.
deliverables: `main.cpp` with a `Student` struct and a working add/list/quit menu
Input validation that survives bad input without crashing
A README with build and run instructions
A short terminal recording or screenshots showing the menu in use
done_when: The program compiles with `-Wall -Wextra` and shows no warnings
Adding several students and choosing 'Show All' lists them correctly
Typing letters where a number is expected does not crash the program
Choosing Quit exits cleanly
hints: If your program crashes on bad input, check `std::cin.fail()` and call `std::cin.clear(); std::cin.ignore(...)` to recover.
Pass vectors as `const std::vector<Student>&` when you only read them — it's faster and documents intent.
[cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/) is the best place to look up any standard function or container.
1.stretch: Add a 'Show Top Scorer' menu option that finds the student with the highest marks.
post_highlights: Built a C++ command-line tool using structs and std::vector to manage records
Wrote input validation that keeps the program running on bad input
Compiled clean with -Wall -Wextra and no warnings

2.title: Classes, File Saving and Sorting
2.goal: Turn your struct into a proper class with encapsulated data, save and load records to a file so nothing is lost between runs, and add search and sort features using the STL.
learn: Classes with private members, constructors and getter methods
Reading and writing plain text files with `std::ifstream` / `std::ofstream`
`std::sort` with a custom comparator (lambda)
Linear search with `std::find_if`
Splitting code into a `.h` header and `.cpp` source file
steps: Convert `Student` into a class with private fields and a constructor, plus `getName()`, `getMarks()` etc.
Move the class into `Student.h`/`Student.cpp` and keep `main.cpp` focused on the menu.
Write `saveToFile(path)` that writes one comma-separated line per student, and `loadFromFile(path)` that rebuilds the vector on startup.
Add a 'Sort by Marks' option using `std::sort(vec.begin(), vec.end(), [](auto&a, auto&b){ return a.getMarks() > b.getMarks(); })`.
Add a 'Search by Name' option using `std::find_if` with a lambda that compares names.
Re-test every Week 1 menu option to make sure splitting the code into files didn't break anything.
Handle the case where the save file doesn't exist yet on first run (create it instead of crashing).
Update the README with the new file format and menu options.
deliverables: A `Student` class in its own header/source files with encapsulated data
Save/load to a text file so data survives between runs
Sort-by-marks and search-by-name menu options
An updated README describing the saved file format
done_when: Adding students, quitting, and restarting the program shows the same data
Sort by Marks lists students highest-to-lowest correctly
Search by Name finds a student even with partial or different-case input handled sensibly
The program still runs cleanly if the save file is missing
hints: Keep the file format simple: one field per comma, one student per line — you can always improve it later.
A lambda like `[](const Student&a, const Student&b){ return a.getMarks() > b.getMarks(); }` is exactly what `std::sort`'s third argument wants.
Test save/load with just 2-3 students first before trusting it with more.
2.stretch: Support multiple save 'profiles' by asking for a filename at startup instead of hardcoding one.
post_highlights: Refactored a C++ CLI tool into a proper class with file-based persistence
Implemented sorting and searching using the STL (std::sort, std::find_if, lambdas)
Split code across header and source files for a cleaner project structure

3.title: A Hand-Built Data Structure and Recursion
3.goal: Add a feature that needs a data structure or algorithm you implement yourself, not just an STL call, so you understand what's happening underneath. You'll add a simple linked-list based history log and a recursive search or sort.
learn: Implementing a singly linked list from scratch (nodes and pointers)
Recursion, using it to implement binary search or merge sort by hand
Time complexity basics (why binary search is O(log n) vs linear O(n))
Smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`) as a safer alternative to raw `new`/`delete`
Basic exception handling with `try`/`catch`
steps: Design a simple `HistoryNode` linked list (using `std::unique_ptr<HistoryNode> next`) that logs every add/edit/delete action as a string with a timestamp.
Add a 'Show History' menu option that walks the linked list and prints every entry in order.
Implement binary search by hand (recursive or iterative) over your marks-sorted vector, and compare its result against `std::find_if` to check correctness.
Write a short recursive function (e.g. merge sort, or a recursive sum/average) and use it in at least one feature, with a comment explaining the base case and recursive case.
Wrap file operations in `try`/`catch` and print a friendly error message instead of crashing if the file can't be opened.
Time your binary search against a linear search on a larger generated dataset (50-100 students) and print both timings to see the difference.
Make sure there are no memory leaks: if you use any raw `new`, replace it with `std::unique_ptr` or a container.
Update the README with a short paragraph explaining your linked list and why binary search needs sorted data.
deliverables: A hand-built singly linked list tracking an action history
A hand-written binary search (or merge sort) used somewhere in the app
try/catch error handling around file operations
A short written comparison of binary search vs linear search timing
done_when: Show History correctly lists actions in the order they happened
Your binary search returns the same result as a linear search on the same sorted data
Deliberately breaking the save file (or removing write permission) shows a friendly message instead of a crash
No raw `new` without a matching `delete` or a smart pointer remains in the code
hints: Draw your linked list on paper first — get the pointer connections right before typing code.
Binary search bugs are almost always off-by-one errors in the `low`/`high`/`mid` bounds — trace through a 3-element example by hand.
`std::unique_ptr` deletes its memory automatically when it goes out of scope, which is why it avoids most leaks.
3.stretch: Add an 'Undo last action' feature that pops the most recent entry off your history and reverses it.
post_highlights: Implemented a linked list and binary search from scratch in C++
Added error handling with try/catch and replaced raw pointers with smart pointers
Measured and compared binary search vs linear search performance

4.title: Polish, Bulk Import and a Final Report
4.goal: Finish the project with a feature that ties everything together: importing many records at once from a CSV file, generating a summary report, and cleaning up the codebase for a strong final demo.
learn: Reading and parsing a CSV file with `std::stringstream`
Generating a formatted text report (averages, min/max, grade distribution)
Basic unit testing by writing small standalone test functions
Code cleanup: consistent naming, removing dead code, adding comments
steps: Write an `importFromCSV(path)` function that reads a CSV of students using `std::stringstream` to split each line, and reports how many rows succeeded or were skipped as invalid.
Add a 'Generate Report' option that prints class average, highest/lowest scorer, and a simple grade distribution (A/B/C/D counts).
Write 4-5 small test functions (e.g. `testBinarySearch()`, `testSort()`) that check known inputs against expected outputs and print PASS/FAIL, called from a `--test` command-line flag.
Do a full read-through of your code: rename any unclear variables, remove commented-out old code, and add a short comment above every function explaining what it does.
Test the whole program end-to-end: import a CSV, sort, search, generate a report, check history, and save.
Time-box one polish item — better table formatting, coloured terminal output, or a progress message during import.
Write a final README section: what the project does, how to build it, how to run the tests, and 2-3 screenshots.
Record a 30-60 second demo showing import, a search, a sort, and the final report.
deliverables: CSV bulk import with a summary of successes/skipped rows
A 'Generate Report' feature with averages and grade distribution
At least 4 small self-checking test functions runnable via a `--test` flag
A polished README with build/run/test instructions and screenshots
done_when: Importing a CSV with a few deliberately bad rows still loads the good ones and reports the bad ones
The generated report's average matches a manual calculation on the same data
Running with `--test` prints PASS for every test function
The code compiles warning-free and has no leftover debug prints or dead code
hints: `std::stringstream` plus `std::getline(ss, field, ',')` is the simplest way to split a CSV line without a library.
Keep your test functions tiny and obvious — a test you can't trust is worse than no test.
Doing the polish pass last, after everything works, keeps you from over-engineering earlier weeks.
4.stretch: Export the generated report to a `.txt` or `.csv` file instead of only printing it to the terminal.
post_highlights: Added CSV bulk import and an automated summary report to a C++ CLI tool
Wrote self-checking test functions to verify core logic
Polished and documented a 4-week C++ project from scratch to a working demo

tracks.tagline: Build a small ASCII/terminal-based 2D game in C++, adding movement, collisions and simple physics week by week.

1.title: A Moving Character on a Grid
1.goal: Draw a simple grid in the terminal and make a character move on it using keyboard input. This is the smallest playable slice of the game and sets up the structure every later week extends.
learn: Representing a 2D grid with a `std::vector<std::vector<char>>`
Reading single keypresses in a loop (or turn-based input with `std::cin`)
Basic 2D coordinates and updating a position (`x`, `y`)
Clearing and redrawing the terminal screen each frame/turn
steps: Pick a simple input style to start: turn-based (press Enter after each move) is fine and much easier than real-time key capture.
Create a `Grid` of fixed size (e.g. 10x10) filled with `.` characters, and a player position `(x, y)` marked with `@`.
Write a `draw(grid)` function that prints the whole grid to the terminal each turn.
Read a direction from the user (`w/a/s/d`) and update the player's `x`/`y`, checking the new position stays inside the grid bounds.
Add a `system("cls")` (Windows) or `system("clear")` (Mac/Linux) call before each redraw so the grid doesn't scroll endlessly.
Place a static goal tile `G` somewhere on the grid and print a win message when the player reaches it.
Add a move counter and print it each turn.
Commit your code with a README describing the controls.
deliverables: A working terminal grid game where a character can move with w/a/s/d
Boundary checking so the player can't move off the grid
A goal tile and win condition
A README explaining the controls and how to run the game
done_when: The player can move in all four directions and the grid redraws correctly each turn
Trying to move off the edge of the grid is blocked, not crashed or wrapped
Reaching the goal tile prints a clear win message and the game ends
The move counter increases by exactly one per valid move
hints: Turn-based input (press a key, then Enter) is much simpler to get right than real-time key capture — start there and only look at libraries like `conio.h`/ncurses later if you want real-time movement as a stretch.
Store the grid as rows of characters and remember `grid[y][x]`, not `grid[x][y]` — mixing this up is the most common bug.
[cppreference on std::vector](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector) is worth a skim if 2D vectors feel unfamiliar.
1.stretch: Add a second, randomly-placed goal tile and track which one is closer to the player.
post_highlights: Built a terminal-based 2D grid game in C++ with keyboard-controlled movement
Implemented boundary checking and a win condition on a custom grid
Designed a simple turn-based game loop with redraw and move tracking

2.title: Obstacles, Collisions and Classes
2.goal: Add obstacles the player must avoid, detect collisions, and refactor the game into classes so the code stays organised as features grow.
learn: Designing a `Player` class and an `Entity`/`Obstacle` class
Collision detection by comparing coordinates
Using `std::vector` to manage a list of obstacles
Randomly placing items on a grid without overlapping the player or each other
steps: Create a `Player` class holding position and a `move(dx, dy)` method that respects grid bounds.
Create an `Obstacle` struct/class with a position and a symbol (e.g. `#`).
Generate 5-8 obstacles at random grid positions at game start, making sure none overlap the player's start position, each other, or the goal.
In the move logic, check if the player's new position matches any obstacle; if so, block the move (or end the game — your choice, but document it).
Add a 'lives' counter: if you choose to end the game on collision, give the player 3 lives and only end after all are lost.
Refactor `draw()` to take the player and the obstacle list and render everything together.
Re-test Week 1's win condition to make sure it still works with obstacles added.
Update the README with the new rules (obstacles, lives).
deliverables: Player and Obstacle classes with clean, separated responsibilities
Randomly generated obstacles that don't overlap the player, goal, or each other
Working collision detection with a lives system
An updated README describing the new rules
done_when: Obstacles never spawn on top of the player, the goal, or each other
Colliding with an obstacle correctly reduces lives (or ends the game, per your design)
Losing all lives ends the game with a clear message
The win condition from Week 1 still works correctly
hints: A simple 'try random position, check if taken, retry' loop is enough for non-overlapping placement at this scale.
Keep collision detection as simple integer comparisons (`player.x == obstacle.x && player.y == obstacle.y`) — no need for anything fancier on a grid.
If lives are hard to test, temporarily set lives to 1 while debugging, then change it back.
2.stretch: Add one obstacle that moves one step every turn (even a simple back-and-forth pattern) to make the game feel more alive.
post_highlights: Refactored a terminal game into Player and Obstacle classes
Implemented collision detection with a lives system
Added randomly generated, non-overlapping obstacles to a C++ game

3.title: Simple Physics: Gravity and Velocity
3.goal: Add basic physics so the player has velocity and gravity instead of just teleporting one grid cell per key press — the first real step from 'grid puzzle' toward 'game engine' thinking.
learn: Representing velocity as a change applied each tick instead of an instant jump
A simple fixed-timestep game loop (update, then draw, then sleep briefly)
Basic gravity: velocity increases downward each tick until blocked by the ground/floor
Clamping values (so velocity or position never exceeds sensible limits)
steps: Add a `vy` (vertical velocity) field to `Player`, and a fixed `GRAVITY` constant added to `vy` every tick.

Change movement to a real loop: each tick, apply `vy` to `y`, then apply horizontal input, then check collisions with the ground/obstacles, then redraw. Use `std::this_thread::sleep_for` to pace ticks (e.g. 150ms).
Add a 'jump' key that gives the player a one-time upward `vy` if they are standing on the ground, and let gravity pull them back down.
Clamp the player's `y` so they can't fall through the floor or fly above the grid top.
Test edge cases: jumping repeatedly in the air should do nothing (no double-jump unless you explicitly want that as a feature).
Add a platform or two (a row of `#` the player can land on) partway up the grid, and make sure landing on one stops the fall correctly.
Write down (in the README) the tick rate and gravity value you chose and why, so the pacing is documented.
Re-test Week 1 and Week 2 features (movement, win, obstacles, lives) still work in the new tick-based loop.
deliverables: A tick-based game loop with a fixed timestep
Gravity and jump mechanics using a velocity value
At least one mid-air platform the player can land on
Clamped position values so the player can't leave the grid
done_when: The player falls automatically when not on ground or a platform
Jump only works when standing on something solid, and gravity pulls the player back down afterward
The player cannot fall through the floor or a platform they're standing on
The game loop runs at a steady, visible pace (not instant, not frozen)
hints: Get vertical movement working alone first (ignore horizontal movement) before combining both.
If the player 'jitters' near a platform, it's usually because you check collision before clamping position — apply movement, then correct position, then check.
`std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(150));` needs `#include <thread>` and `#include <chrono>`.
3.stretch: Add a second, higher platform requiring a well-timed double jump input sequence (not necessarily a true double jump mechanic) to reach.
post_highlights: Implemented a tick-based game loop with gravity and jump physics in C++
Added velocity-based movement instead of instant grid teleportation
Built and debugged platform collision for a simple physics system

4.title: Levels, Scoring and a Polished Demo
4.goal: Turn your prototype into a small finished game: add a second level, a scoring system, and polish that makes it demo-ready.
learn: Loading level layouts from a simple text file instead of hardcoding them
A basic scoring system (points for coins collected, time bonus, etc.)
A simple game-state machine (menu → playing → game over → restart)
Writing small test functions to check collision and scoring logic
steps: Design 2 level layouts as plain text files (rows of characters: `.` floor, `#` obstacle/platform, `@` start, `G` goal, `C` coin) and write a `loadLevel(path)` function to read one into your grid.
Add collectible coins (`C`) that disappear and add to a score when the player walks over them.
Add a simple state machine: show a start menu, run the level, then show a 'Game Over / You Win' screen with the final score and a 'play again?' prompt.
Wire up level progression: reaching the goal on level 1 loads level 2; reaching the goal on level 2 shows a final win screen.
Write 3-4 small test functions for your core logic (e.g. collision detection, score addition, gravity clamp) that print PASS/FAIL, runnable via a `--test` flag.
Do a full playtest of both levels start to finish, fixing anything that feels broken or unfair.
Clean up the code: consistent naming, comments on non-obvious logic, remove leftover debug prints.
Write a final README with controls, how to run, how to run tests, and a 30-60 second demo video or screenshots of both levels.
deliverables: Two playable levels loaded from text files
A coin collection and scoring system
A start-menu / playing / game-over state machine
At least 3 self-checking test functions and a polished README
done_when: Both levels load correctly from their text files and are fully playable
Collecting a coin removes it and increases the score exactly once
Finishing level 1 loads level 2, and finishing level 2 shows a final win screen with the score
`--test` prints PASS for every test function, and the code has no leftover debug output
hints: Keep level files tiny at first (5x5) to debug loading before making them bigger.
A `enum class GameState { Menu, Playing, GameOver }` with a `switch` in your main loop is a clean way to manage state transitions.
Playtest with fresh eyes after a break — you'll spot unfair or confusing parts you got used to while building.
4.stretch: Add a simple high-score file that remembers the best score across runs.
post_highlights: Shipped a 2-level terminal game in C++ with physics, coins and scoring
Implemented level loading from text files and a game-state machine
Wrote automated tests for core game logic and polished the project for a public demo

tracks.project_name: DataVault: A Simple In-Memory Database Engine
tracks.tagline: Build a tiny command-line database engine in C++ that stores records, indexes them for fast lookup, and supports simple queries.

1.title: Records, Tables and Basic Commands
1.goal: Build the core of a tiny database: a table that stores key-value style records in memory and a command interface to insert and view them.
learn: Modelling a database 'table' with `std::vector<std::map<std::string, std::string>>`
Parsing simple text commands from user input
String splitting and trimming in C++
Basic error messages for invalid commands instead of crashing
steps: Decide on a simple record shape: each record is a `std::map<std::string, std::string>` (e.g. `{"name": "Asha", "age": "21"}`).
Store all records in a `std::vector` representing one table.
Write a command parser that reads a line like `INSERT name=Asha age=21` and splits it into a command and key=value pairs.
Implement `INSERT`, `SELECT ALL`, and `QUIT` commands in a loop.
Print `SELECT ALL` results as a readable table, aligning columns.
Handle malformed commands (e.g. missing `=`) by printing an error instead of crashing.
Add a `HELP` command listing all supported commands.
Commit your code with a README documenting the command syntax.
deliverables: A working command loop supporting INSERT, SELECT ALL, HELP and QUIT
Records stored as key-value maps in a vector (your 'table')
Friendly error messages for malformed commands
A README documenting every supported command
done_when: INSERT followed by SELECT ALL shows the inserted record correctly
A malformed command shows an error message, not a crash
HELP lists every implemented command
QUIT exits the program cleanly
hints: `std::istringstream` plus `std::getline(ss, token, ' ')` is a simple way to split a command line into tokens.
Keep your first version's columns fixed (name, age) before generalising to arbitrary fields — get something working first.
[cppreference on std::map](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/map) is worth a quick read if maps are new to you.
1.stretch: Support an arbitrary number of key=value fields per record, not just a fixed set.
post_highlights: Built a command-line database engine core in C++ with an INSERT/SELECT command loop
Modelled table records with std::map and std::vector
Implemented a command parser with friendly error handling

2.title: Filtering, Updating and Deleting
2.goal: Add the rest of basic CRUD: filter records with a WHERE-style condition, update matching records, and delete them, plus persist the table to disk.
learn: Filtering a vector of records with a simple condition (`std::copy_if` or a manual loop)
Updating fields in place vs building a new filtered vector
Saving and loading structured data to a text file (a simple custom format)
Separating parsing logic from execution logic (a `Command` struct)
steps: Extend the parser to support `SELECT WHERE field=value`, `UPDATE WHERE field=value SET field2=value2`, and `DELETE WHERE field=value`.
Implement `SELECT WHERE` by looping through records and printing only matches.
Implement `UPDATE WHERE ... SET ...` by looping through matches and modifying their map in place.
Implement `DELETE WHERE` using `std::vector::erase` with a condition (or building a new vector of the ones that don't match, which is often simpler to get right).
Write `saveTable(path)` and `loadTable(path)` using a simple line-based format (e.g. one record per line, fields separated by `;`, key=value within).
Load the table automatically on startup if the save file exists, and save automatically on QUIT.
Re-test every Week 1 command to make sure nothing broke.
Update the README with the new command syntax and file format.
deliverables: Working SELECT WHERE, UPDATE WHERE ... SET, and DELETE WHERE commands
Save-on-quit and load-on-start persistence to a text file
A documented on-disk file format
Regression-tested Week 1 commands still working
done_when: SELECT WHERE returns only records matching the condition
UPDATE WHERE correctly changes only the matching records' specified field
DELETE WHERE removes exactly the matching records and no others
Restarting the program after QUIT shows the same data as before
hints: Building a new vector of records you want to KEEP is often less error-prone than erasing in place while iterating.
Test WHERE conditions with a small dataset (3-4 records) where you know by hand exactly which should match.
If your load function silently produces an empty table, print the number of records loaded to catch parsing bugs early.
2.stretch: Support a second condition with AND, e.g. `SELECT WHERE age=21 AND name=Asha`.
post_highlights: Implemented UPDATE and DELETE with WHERE-style filtering in a custom C++ database engine
Added file-based persistence with a custom save/load format
Extended a command parser to support conditional queries

3.title: Indexing for Fast Lookup
3.goal: Add an index so lookups by a chosen field are fast instead of scanning every record, and measure the speed difference — the core idea behind how real databases work.
learn: Why linear scans get slow as data grows, and what an index trades off (memory for speed)
Using `std::unordered_map` to build a hash-based index
Keeping an index in sync when records are inserted, updated or deleted
Basic timing/benchmarking with `<chrono>`
steps: Pick one field to index first (e.g. `name`) and build a `std::unordered_map<std::string, std::vector<int>>` mapping value to record positions.
Rebuild the index whenever the table is loaded, and update it incrementally on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE so it never goes stale.
Add a `SELECT WHERE name=X` fast path that checks the index first instead of scanning every record, while keeping the slow scan as a fallback for other fields.
Generate a larger test dataset (1000+ records) with a small script or loop, and time indexed vs non-indexed lookups using `<chrono>`.
Print both timings so the speed difference is visible in your demo.
Write a short paragraph in the README explaining, in your own words, why the indexed lookup is faster.
Add an `INDEX field` command that lets the user build an index on a different field at runtime.
Re-test all Week 1-2 commands with the index in place to make sure it never goes out of sync with the data.
deliverables: A hash-based index on at least one field, kept in sync with the data
A fast lookup path that uses the index when available
A timing comparison between indexed and non-indexed lookups on 1000+ records
A short written explanation of why the index is faster
done_when: Indexed lookups return exactly the same results as a full scan on the same data
The index stays correct after INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operations
The timing test clearly shows the indexed lookup is faster on a large dataset
The INDEX command can build an index on a different field at runtime
hints: If your index goes out of sync, it's almost always because you forgot to update it in one of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — check all three.
1000 records generated with a loop (`name + std::to_string(i)`) is plenty to see a clear timing difference; you don't need real data.
`std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now()` before and after, then subtract, gives you an easy duration to print.
3.stretch: Support indexing on more than one field at a time and let SELECT WHERE pick whichever index is available.
post_highlights: Built a hash-based index in C++ to speed up record lookups
Measured and demonstrated the performance difference between indexed and linear-scan queries
Kept an index correctly synced across insert, update and delete operations

4.title: Multiple Tables, Tests and a Final Demo
4.goal: Extend your engine to support more than one table, add automated tests for your core logic, and polish the project into a demo-ready mini database.
learn: Managing multiple named tables in one engine (`std::map<std::string, Table>`)
A `CREATE TABLE` / `USE TABLE` style command set
Writing small, focused unit tests for core logic (insert, index, query)
Final code cleanup and documentation for a public-facing project
steps: Refactor your single table into a `Table` class, and store multiple named tables in a `std::map<std::string, Table>`.
Add `CREATE TABLE name` and `USE TABLE name` commands so the user can switch which table subsequent commands apply to.
Make sure save/load now handles multiple tables (e.g. one file per table, or one combined file with table markers).
Write 5-6 small test functions covering insert, WHERE filtering, update, delete, and indexed lookup correctness, runnable via a `--test` flag, each printing PASS/FAIL.
Do a full walkthrough: create two tables, insert into both, query each, save, restart, and confirm both tables reload correctly.
Clean up the codebase: consistent naming, comments on tricky logic, remove any leftover debug prints or commented-out code.
Write a final README covering all commands, the file format, how to run tests, and a short architecture overview (table → records → index).
Record a 30-60 second demo showing multiple tables, a query using the index, and a timing comparison.
deliverables: Support for multiple named tables with CREATE TABLE / USE TABLE
Persistence that correctly saves and loads multiple tables
At least 5 automated test functions covering core engine logic
A polished README with full command reference and architecture overview
done_when: Two or more tables can be created, populated and queried independently without interfering with each other
Restarting the program restores all tables correctly from disk
Running with `--test` prints PASS for every test function
The README fully documents every command and the on-disk format
hints: Get multi-table save/load working with a tiny example (2 tables, 1 record each) before trusting it with real data.
If tests are hard to write for indexed lookups, first assert they match a plain linear scan on the same query — that's a strong correctness check.
Save the polish pass for last; a working, well-documented simple engine beats a half-finished complex one.
4.stretch: Add a simple `JOIN`-like command that combines matching records from two tables on a shared field.
post_highlights: Extended a C++ database engine to support multiple tables with CREATE/USE commands
Wrote automated tests covering insert, query, update, delete and index correctness
Shipped a documented, demo-ready mini database engine built from scratch in C++
